1.title: Short title, application and commencement
1.text: Defines the title, applicability to judicial proceedings (effective July 1, 2024, vide notification No. S.O. 849(E)), and excludes affidavits and arbitration.

2.title: Definitions
2.text: Provides comprehensive definitions for terms like "Court," "document," "evidence," and "fact," incorporating electronic records and aligning with modern legal frameworks.

3.title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts
3.text: Limits admissible evidence to facts in issue and those declared relevant, ensuring compliance with civil procedure laws.

4.title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction
4.text: Admits facts closely connected to the transaction, regardless of time or place, to provide context.

5.title: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts
5.text: Admits facts that set the stage, cause, or result from facts in issue, providing critical context for understanding events.

6.title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct
6.text: Establishes relevancy of motive, preparation, and conduct (previous or subsequent) that influences or is influenced by facts in issue, with statements affecting conduct also admissible.

7.title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce relevant facts
7.text: Allows facts that clarify, introduce, or contextualize relevant facts, such as identity, timing, or party relationships, to be admitted as necessary.

8.title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design
8.text: Makes statements or actions by co-conspirators relevant against all conspirators if done in furtherance of a common intention, provided a reasonable belief in the conspiracy exists.

9.title: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant
9.text: Permits otherwise irrelevant facts if they contradict or significantly affect the probability of facts in issue or relevant facts, such as alibis.

10.title: Facts tending to enable Court to determine amount are relevant in suits for damages.

11.title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question
11.text: Specifies that transactions or instances related to the creation, claim, modification, recognition, assertion, denial, or inconsistency with a right or custom are relevant when its existence is questioned.

12.title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling
12.text: Facts indicating a person’s state of mind (e.g., intention, knowledge, good faith) or body (e.g., health, sensations) are relevant when such states are in issue. The state of mind must pertain to the specific matter in question, and previous convictions may be relevant in criminal trials.

13.title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional
13.text: Evidence of a series of similar acts by the same person is relevant to determine whether an act was accidental or intentional, or done with specific knowledge or intent.

14.title: Existence of course of business when relevant
14.text: The usual course of business that naturally leads to an act being performed is relevant when the occurrence of that act is in question.

15.title: Admission defined
15.text: Defines an admission as a statement (oral, written, or electronic) that implies a fact in issue or relevant fact, made by specific persons under conditions outlined in subsequent sections.

16.title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent
16.text: Admissions include statements by a party or their authorized agent, or by persons with a proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject matter, made during the period of their interest. Statements by representative parties are not admissions unless made in that capacity.

17.title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit
17.text: Statements by individuals whose position or liability must be proven against a party are considered admissions if made while they hold that position or liability and would be relevant in a suit involving them.

18.title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit
18.text: Statements by individuals explicitly referred to by a party for information on a disputed matter are treated as admissions.

19.title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf
19.text: Admissions can be used against the maker or their representative but not by them, except when they would be admissible under Section 26 if the maker were dead, reflect a relevant state of mind or body with corroborating conduct, or are relevant for another purpose.

20.title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant
20.text: Oral admissions about a document’s contents are inadmissible unless the unless secondary evidence is permissible or the document’s authenticity is disputed.

21.title: Admissions in civil cases when relevant
21.text: Nothing in this section shall be taken to exempt any advocate from giving evidence of any matter of which he may be compelled to give evidence under section 132. Explanation : Admissions in civil cases are not relevant if made under an express condition of non-disclosure or an implied agreement between parties to exclude them as evidence. Advocates are not exempt from testifying under Section 132.

22.title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding
22.text: Confessions obtained through inducement, threats, coercion, or promises from a person in authority are inadmissible in criminal proceedings if they suggest an advantage or avoidance of harm. Confessions made in police custody, if recorded immediately in writing or via audio-video means, are not considered coerced despite handcuffs.

23.title: Confession to police officer
23.text: Confessions made to a police officer or in police custody are generally inadmissible unless made in a Magistrate’s presence. Information leading to the discovery of a fact is admissible, even if part of a confession.

24.title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence
24.text: A confession by one accused implicating themselves and co-accused in a joint trial for the same offence (including abetment or attempt) can be considered against both.

25.title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop
25.text: Admissions are not definitive proof but can prevent the maker from denying the admitted facts under estoppel rules.

26.title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant
26.text: Statements by persons who are dead, untraceable, incapacitated, or whose attendance is unreasonably difficult to procure are relevant in cases such as dying declarations, business records, statements against interest, opinions on public rights, or family relationships, provided specific conditions are met.

27.title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, the truth of facts therein stated
27.text: A criminal trial or inquiry shall be deemed to be a proceeding between the prosecutor and the accused within the meaning of this section. Explanation : Prior testimony from a judicial or authorized proceeding is admissible in later proceedings to prove stated facts if the witness is unavailable, provided the parties, issues, and cross-examination opportunities are substantially the same.

28.title: Entries in books of account when relevant
28.text: Regularly maintained business account entries, including electronic records, are relevant but insufficient alone to establish liability.

29.title: Relevancy of entry in public record or an electronic record made in performance of duty
29.text: Entries in official or public records, including electronic ones, made by public servants or others in their legal duties are relevant facts.

30.title: Relevancy of statements in maps, charts and plans
30.text: Statements in publicly sold or government-authorized maps, charts, or plans are relevant facts.

31.title: Relevancy of statement as to fact of public nature contained in certain Acts or notifications
31.text: Statements about public facts in Central/State Acts, government notifications, or certain gazettes are relevant when the Court assesses such facts.

32.title: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books
32.text: Statements of foreign law in government-authorized books or court ruling reports are relevant when the Court evaluates such laws.

33.title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers
33.text: When a statement is part of a broader context (conversation, document, electronic record, book, or series), only the portion necessary for understanding its nature and context should be presented as evidence.

34.title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial
34.text: A previous judgment, order, or decree that legally bars a court from proceeding with a second suit or trial is considered a relevant fact when determining whether the court should take cognizance of such suit or trial.

35.title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction
35.text: Judgments in probate, matrimonial, admiralty, or insolvency cases that establish or remove legal status or absolute rights are relevant and conclusive proof of such status or rights from the specified times.

36.title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35
36.text: Judgments outside Section 35’s scope are relevant for public matters but not conclusive proof of their contents.

37.title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36, when relevant
37.text: Judgments not covered by Sections 34, 35, or 36 are irrelevant unless their existence is a fact in issue or relevant under another provision.

38.title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved
38.text: Parties can challenge relevant judgments under Sections 34, 35, or 36 by proving the Court lacked jurisdiction or the judgment was obtained fraudulently or collusively.

39.title: Opinions of experts
39.text: Expert opinions on foreign law, science, art, handwriting, or fingerprints are relevant when the Court needs to form an opinion on these matters.

40.title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts
40.text: Facts supporting or contradicting expert opinions are relevant when those opinions are admissible.

41.title: Opinion as to handwriting, when relevant
41.text: A person is said to be acquainted with the handwriting of another person when he has seen that person write, or when he has received documents purporting to be written by that person in answer to documents written by himself or under his authority and addressed to that person, or when, in the ordinary course of business, documents purporting to be written by that person have been habitually submitted to him. Illustration : The question is, whether a given letter is in the handwriting of A, a merchant in London. B is a merchant in Kolkata, who has written letters addressed to A and received let

42.title: Opinion as to existence of right or custom, when relevant
42.text: The expression “general custom or right” includes customs or rights common to any considerable class of persons. Illustration : The right of the villagers of a particular village to use the water of a particular well is a general right within the meaning of this section. Explanation : Opinions of knowledgeable persons about general customs or rights affecting a significant group are relevant.

43.title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant
43.text: Opinions of those with specialized knowledge about group usages, religious/charitable institutions, or regional/class-specific terms are relevant.

44.title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant
44.text: Opinions expressed through conduct by those with special knowledge (e.g., family members) about relationships are relevant, but insufficient alone to prove marriage in specific legal proceedings.

45.title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant
45.text: The basis for a living person’s relevant opinion, such as experiments or observations, is also relevant.

46.title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant
46.text: In civil cases, a person’s character is irrelevant to prove likely conduct unless it arises from other relevant facts.

47.title: In criminal cases previous good character relevant
47.text: Evidence of an accused’s good character is relevant in criminal cases.

48.title: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases
48.text: An accused’s bad character is irrelevant in criminal cases unless good character evidence is introduced, or bad character is a fact in issue. Previous convictions indicate bad character.

49.title: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply
49.text: An accused’s bad character is irrelevant in criminal cases unless good character evidence is introduced, or bad character is a fact in issue. Previous convictions indicate bad character.

50.title: Character as affecting damages
50.text: In sections 46, 47, 48 and this section, the word “character” includes both reputation and disposition; but, except as provided in section 48, evidence may be given only of general reputation and general disposition, and not of particular acts by which reputation or disposition were shown. Explanation : In civil cases, a person’s character (reputation and disposition) is relevant for assessing damages. Evidence is limited to general reputation/disposition, not specific acts, except as per Section 48.

51.title: Facts judicially noticeable need not be proved
51.text: This section states that facts which the court can take judicial notice of, such as public and well-known facts, do not require formal proof.
51.chapter: Chapter III: Facts which need not be proved (Sections 51-53)

52.title: Facts of which Court must take judicial notice
52.text: Lists specific facts, such as laws, treaties, and public holidays, that courts must take judicial notice of, and allows courts to refer to reliable sources for matters of public history, literature, science, or art.
52.chapter: Chapter III: Facts which need not be proved (Sections 51-53)

53.title: Facts admitted need not be proved
53.text: States that facts admitted by parties, either at the hearing, in writing, or through pleadings, do not need to be proved, unless the court, in its discretion, requires further proof.
53.chapter: Chapter III: Facts which need not be proved (Sections 51-53)

54.title: Proof of facts by oral evidence
54.text: This section specifies that oral evidence can be used to prove all facts except those contained in documents or electronic records, which require specific forms of proof.

55.title: Oral evidence to be direct
55.text: Requires oral evidence to be direct, meaning it must come from a witness who personally saw, heard, or perceived the fact, or holds the opinion being presented, with provisions for expert treatises and material inspection.

56.title: Proof of contents of documents
56.text: This section allows the contents of documents to be proved using either primary evidence (original documents) or secondary evidence (copies or other forms) as per the provisions of the Act.

57.title: Primary evidence
57.text: Defines primary evidence as the original document presented to the court, with explanations for documents executed in parts, counterparts, or through uniform processes like printing.

58.title: Secondary evidence
58.text: Defines secondary evidence, including certified copies, mechanically produced copies, and oral accounts by someone who has seen the original, with illustrations clarifying admissible forms.

59.title: Proof of contents of documents by primary or secondary evidence
59.text: Reiterates that document contents can be proved by primary or secondary evidence, subject to the rules outlined in the Act.

60.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given
60.text: Specifies circumstances under which secondary evidence is admissible, such as when the original is lost, destroyed, or in possession of the opposing party who fails to produce it after notice.

61.title: Electronic or digital record
61.text: Outlines the requirement of giving notice to produce a document before secondary evidence can be admitted, with exceptions where notice is not required, such as when the document is a notice itself or the adverse party has obtained it by fraud.

62.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record

63.title: Admissibility of electronic records.
63.text: Mandates that for documents requiring attestation, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution, unless the document is a registered non-will document and execution is not denied.

64.title: Rules as to notice to produce
64.text: Provides for proving execution of an attested document when no attesting witness is available or the document was executed abroad, by verifying the handwriting of the attesting witness and the executor.

65.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produce.
65.text: States that if a party admits to executing an attested document, this admission is sufficient proof of execution against them, even if the document requires attestation.

66.title: Proof as to electronic signature
66.text: Requires proof that an electronic signature belongs to the alleged subscriber, except for secure electronic signatures, which are presumed authentic under the Information Technology Act, 2000. Proof may involve testimony, technical evidence, or expert verification under Section 39. This section aligns with modern digital evidence frameworks, replacing Section 67A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

67.title: Proof of execution of document required by law to be attested
67.text: Mandates that for documents legally requiring attestation, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution, unless the document (except a will) is registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908, and execution is not denied.

68.title: Proof where no attesting witness found
68.text: Provides alternative proof methods when an attesting witness is unavailable or the document was executed abroad, requiring evidence of the attesting witness’s handwriting and the executant’s signature.

69.title: Admission of execution by party to attested document
69.text: Allows a party’s admission of executing an attested document to serve as sufficient proof against them, even if attestation is legally required.

70.title: Proof when attesting witness denies execution
70.text: Permits alternative evidence to prove a document’s execution if the attesting witness denies or cannot recall the execution.

71.title: Proof of document not required by law to be attested
71.text: Allows documents with attestation, but not legally requiring it, to be proved as if unattested, simplifying the proof process.

72.title: Comparison of signature, writing or seal with others admitted or proved
72.text: Permits courts to compare a disputed signature, writing, or seal with an admitted or proved sample to verify authenticity, even if the sample was not submitted for another purpose.

73.title: Proof as to verification of digital signature
73.text: Allows courts to verify digital signatures by ordering production of Digital Signature Certificates or verification using public keys, referencing the Information Technology Act, 2000.

74.title: Public and private documents
74.text: Defines public documents as those forming acts or records of sovereign authorities, official bodies, or public officers, and private documents as all others.

75.title: Certified copies of public documents
75.text: Requires public officers to provide certified copies of public documents upon request and payment, with proper certification for evidentiary use.

76.title: Proof of documents by production of certified copies
76.text: Allows certified copies of public documents to be used as evidence of their contents.

77.title: Proof of other official documents
77.text: Specifies methods for proving various types of public documents, including government records, legislative proceedings, and foreign documents, through certified copies or official publications.

78.title: Presumption as to genuineness of certified copies
78.text: Establishes a presumption of genuineness for certified copies and certificates issued by authorized officers, provided they comply with legal form and execution requirements.

79.title: Presumption as to documents produced as record of evidence, etc.
79.text: Presumes the genuineness and proper execution of court records, witness statements, or confessions signed by authorized judicial officers.

80.title: Presumption as to Gazettes, newspapers, and other documents
80.text: Presumes the genuineness of Official Gazettes, newspapers, and legally mandated records kept in proper form and custody.

81.title: Presumption as to Gazettes in electronic or digital record
81.text: Extends the presumption of genuineness to electronic or digital Official Gazettes and legally mandated digital records, provided they are in proper form and custody.

82.title: Presumption as to maps or plans made by authority of Government
82.text: Presumes the authenticity and accuracy of government-made maps or plans, except those made for specific legal proceedings, which require proof of accuracy.

83.title: Presumption as to collections of laws and reports of decisions
83.text: Presumes the genuineness of government-published legal texts and court decision reports.

84.title: Presumption as to powers-of-attorney
84.text: Presumes the proper execution and authentication of powers-of-attorney certified by specified authorities.

85.title: Presumption as to electronic agreements
85.text: Presumes the validity of electronic agreements with electronic signatures, aligning with digital contract frameworks under the Information Technology Act, 2000.

86.title: Presumption as to electronic records and electronic signatures
86.text: Presumes the integrity of secure electronic records and the intent behind secure electronic signatures, unless disproved, per the Information Technology Act, 2000.

87.title: Presumption as to Electronic Signature Certificates
87.text: Presumes the accuracy of information in Electronic Signature Certificates, except unverified subscriber details, if accepted by the subscriber.

88.title: Presumption as to certified copies of foreign judicial records
88.text: Allows courts to presume the genuineness of certified copies of foreign judicial records, based on certification methods verified by Indian representatives.

89.title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts
89.text: Presumes the authenticity of books, maps, or charts used for public or general information, based on their stated authorship and publication details.

90.title: Presumption as to electronic messages
90.text: Presumes the content integrity of electronic messages sent via email servers, but requires evidence to prove the sender’s identity.

91.title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced
91.text: Presumes proper execution of documents not produced after a notice to produce, assuming compliance with legal formalities.

92.title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old
92.text: Presumes the authenticity and proper execution of documents at least thirty years old, provided they come from proper custody.

93.title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old
93.text: Presumes the authenticity of electronic signatures on electronic records at least five years old, provided they come from proper custody, aligning with digital evidence frameworks.

94.title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document
94.text: Mandates that written contracts, grants, or property dispositions, or legally required written matters, be proved by the document or admissible secondary evidence, with an exception for public officer appointments.
94.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

95.title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement
95.text: Prohibits oral evidence contradicting or varying written terms, with exceptions for fraud, separate agreements, or customs, ensuring documentary evidence prevails.
95.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

96.title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document
96.text: Prohibits extrinsic evidence to clarify or amend a document’s ambiguous or defective language, preserving its original form.
96.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

97.title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts
97.text: Prevents evidence contradicting a document’s clear language that accurately applies to existing facts, ensuring its intended application.
97.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

98.title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts
98.text: Allows evidence to clarify a document’s plain language that is inapplicable to existing facts by showing its intended peculiar sense.
98.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

99.title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons
99.text: Permits evidence to resolve ambiguity in a document’s language that could apply to one of several persons or things, clarifying the intended subject.
99.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

100.title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies
100.text: Allows evidence to clarify which set of facts a document’s language was intended to apply to when it partially fits multiple scenarios but fully fits none.
100.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

101.title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc.
101.text: Permits evidence to clarify the meaning of illegible characters, specialized terms, or ambiguous expressions in a document.
101.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

102.title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document
102.text: Allows non-parties or their representatives to provide evidence of contemporaneous agreements varying a document’s terms, unlike parties bound by Section 95.
102.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

103.title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills
103.text: Ensures that the rules in this chapter do not override the Indian Succession Act, 1925, regarding the interpretation and construction of wills.
103.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Exclusion of Oral by Documentary Evidence (Sections 94-103)

104.title: Burden of proof
104.text: Places the burden of proof on the person asserting facts to establish a legal right or liability, ensuring they substantiate their claims.
104.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

105.title: On whom burden of proof lies
105.text: Assigns the burden of proof to the party who would lose if no evidence is presented, clarifying responsibility in disputes.
105.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

106.title: Burden of proof as to particular fact
106.text: Requires the party asserting a specific fact to prove it, unless a law specifies otherwise, ensuring targeted evidence.
106.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

107.title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible
107.text: Places the burden on the party seeking to introduce evidence to prove foundational facts required for its admissibility.
107.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

108.title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions
108.text: Shifts the burden to the accused to prove circumstances qualifying for exceptions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or other laws, with a presumption against such circumstances.
108.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

109.title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge
109.text: Assigns the burden of proof to the person with unique knowledge of a fact, ensuring accountability for exclusive information.
109.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

110.title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years
110.text: Presumes a person alive within the last thirty years remains alive unless proven dead, placing the burden on the party claiming death.
110.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

111.title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years
111.text: Shifts the burden to prove a person is alive if they have not been heard from for seven years by those who would likely know, presuming death otherwise.
111.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

112.title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent
112.text: Presumes ongoing relationships like partnership, tenancy, or agency if shown to exist, requiring the party denying or claiming cessation to prove it.
112.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

113.title: Burden of proof as to ownership
113.text: Presumes a person in possession of property is the owner, placing the burden on the challenger to prove otherwise, protecting possessory rights.
113.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

114.title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence
114.text: Requires the party in a position of trust (e.g., fiduciary) to prove good faith in transactions, protecting vulnerable parties.
114.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

115.title: Presumption as to certain offences
115.text: Presumes guilt for specific offences in disturbed areas involving firearms or explosives against public forces, unless disproved, aligning with Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
115.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

116.title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy
116.text: Presumes legitimacy of a child born during a valid marriage or within 280 days of its dissolution, unless non-access between parents is proven.
116.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

117.title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman
117.text: Presumes abetment of suicide by a married woman within seven years of marriage if cruelty by her husband or his relatives is shown, with “cruelty” defined per Section 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
117.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

118.title: Presumption as to dowry death
118.text: Presumes a person caused dowry death if the woman was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry soon before her death, with “dowry death” defined per Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
118.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

119.title: Court may presume existence of certain facts
119.text: Allows courts to presume certain facts based on natural events, human conduct, and business practices, with illustrations guiding application and exceptions.
119.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

120.title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape
120.text: Presumes absence of consent in rape cases under Section 64(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, if the woman testifies to non-consent, with “sexual intercourse” defined per Section 63.
120.chapter: Chapter VII: Of the Burden of Proof (Sections 104-120)

122.title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession
122.text: Prohibits tenants or their successors from denying the landlord’s title during tenancy and licensees from denying the licensor’s title at the time the licence was granted.

123.title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee
123.text: Prevents acceptors of bills of exchange from denying the drawer’s authority, and bailees or licensees from denying the bailor’s or licensor’s authority at the start of bailment or licence, with exceptions for proving the bill’s authenticity or third-party rights.

124.title: Who may testify
124.text: Declares all persons competent to testify unless they cannot understand questions or give rational answers due to age, disease, or similar causes, with a specific note that mental illness does not disqualify unless it impairs understanding or rational responses.

125.title: Witness unable to communicate verbally
125.text: Allows witnesses unable to speak to testify through writing or signs in open court, deemed oral evidence, with a requirement for interpreter or special educator assistance and video recording for non-verbal communication.

126.title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases
126.text: Permits spouses to testify in civil proceedings as parties or witnesses and in criminal proceedings against their spouse.

127.title: Judges and Magistrates
127.text: Prohibits compelling judges or magistrates to testify about their judicial conduct or knowledge gained in court, except by order of a superior court, but allows examination on other matters occurring in their presence.

128.title: Communications during marriage
128.text: Protects marital communications from compelled disclosure unless consented to by the communicator or in cases involving suits or crimes between spouses.

129.title: Evidence as to affairs of State
129.text: Restricts evidence from unpublished official records without permission from the department head.

130.title: Official communications
130.text: Exempts magistrates, police, and revenue officers from disclosing sources of information about offences or revenue violations.

131.title: Information as to commission of offences
131.text: Protects Magistrates, police, and revenue officers from disclosing sources of information about offences.

132.title: Professional communications
132.text: Prohibits advocates from disclosing client communications without consent, except for communications furthering illegal purposes or facts indicating crimes committed during service; extends to interpreters and clerks.

133.title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence
133.text: Clarifies that giving evidence does not waive advocate-client privilege unless the advocate is questioned on protected matters.

134.title: Confidential communication with legal advisers
134.text: Protects confidential communications with legal advisers from disclosure, except when the client testifies and disclosure is necessary to explain their evidence.

135.title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party
135.text: Protects non-party witnesses from producing title-deeds or documents that could incriminate them, unless agreed in writing.

136.title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce
136.text: Prevents compelling production of documents or electronic records if another person could refuse their production, unless consented to.

137.title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate
137.text: Requires witnesses to answer relevant questions even if incriminating, but protects those answers from use in criminal proceedings, except for false evidence.

138.title: Accomplice
138.text: Permits accomplices to testify against accused persons, with convictions valid if supported by corroborated testimony.

139.title: Number of witnesses
139.text: States that no specific number of witnesses is required to prove a fact in any case.

140.title: Order of production and examination of witnesses
140.text: Specifies that the sequence of witness production and examination follows existing civil or criminal procedure laws, or, if absent, is determined by the court’s discretion.
140.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

141.title: Judge to decide as to admissibility of evidence
141.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

142.title: Examination of witnesses
142.text: Defines the three stages of witness examination: examination-in-chief (by the calling party), cross-examination (by the adverse party), and re-examination (by the calling party post-cross-examination).
142.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

143.title: Order of examinations
143.text: Establishes the sequence of witness examinations and their scope, allowing broader cross-examination and limiting re-examination to clarifying cross-examination issues, with provision for additional cross-examination if new matters arise.
143.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

144.title: Cross-examination of person called to produce a document
144.text: Clarifies that producing a document does not make a person a witness subject to cross-examination unless they are formally called as a witness.
144.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

145.title: Witnesses to character
145.text: Permits cross-examination and re-examination of witnesses testifying about a person’s character, ensuring scrutiny of their testimony.
145.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

146.title: Leading questions
146.text: Defines leading questions and restricts their use in examination-in-chief and re-examination without court approval, while allowing them freely in cross-examination, with exceptions for introductory or proven matters.
146.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

147.title: Evidence as to matters in writing
147.text: Allows questioning witnesses about documented matters, requiring document production or secondary evidence justification, while permitting oral evidence of statements about document contents if relevant.
147.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

148.title: Cross-examination as to previous statements in writing
148.text: Permits cross-examination on prior written statements without showing the document, but requires highlighting relevant parts if used to contradict the witness.
148.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

149.title: Questions lawful in cross-examination
149.text: Allows broad cross-examination questions to assess truthfulness, identity, or credibility, even if incriminating, but restricts questions about a victim’s character or sexual history in specific sexual offense cases.
149.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

150.title: When witness to be compelled to answer
150.text: Mandates that witnesses answer relevant questions, subject to protections against self-incrimination as outlined in Section 137.
150.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

151.title: Court to decide when question shall be asked and when witness compelled to answer
151.text: Grants the court discretion to decide whether witnesses must answer non-relevant questions affecting credibility, considering their impact, remoteness, and proportionality, with potential inferences from refusal.
151.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

152.title: Question not to be asked without reasonable grounds
152.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

153.title: Procedure of Court in case of question being asked without reasonable grounds
153.text: Allows the court to report advocates to disciplinary authorities if they ask questions without reasonable grounds, ensuring professional accountability.
153.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

154.title: Indecent and scandalous questions
154.text: Prohibits indecent or scandalous questions unless they directly relate to facts in issue or are essential to resolve those facts, protecting witnesses from inappropriate inquiries.
154.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

155.title: Questions intended to insult or annoy
155.text: Bans questions designed to insult or annoy, or those phrased offensively without necessity, ensuring respectful examination.
155.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

156.title: Exclusion of evidence to contradict answers to questions testing veracity
156.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

157.title: Question by party to his own witness
157.text: Allows a party to question their own witness as if cross-examining, with court permission, without losing the ability to rely on their testimony.
157.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

158.title: Impeaching credit of witness
158.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

159.title: Questions tending to corroborate evidence of relevant fact, admissible
159.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

160.title: Former statements of witness may be proved to corroborate later testimony as to same fact
160.text: Permits proving prior statements made by a witness near the time of the event or before a competent authority to corroborate their current testimony.
160.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

161.title: What matters may be proved in connection with proved statement relevant under section 26 or 27
161.text: Allows proving matters to contradict, corroborate, or assess the credibility of statements under Sections 26 or 27, as if the maker were a witness denying the statement.
161.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

162.title: Refreshing memory
162.text: Permits witnesses to refresh memory using their own or verified writings made near the event, or copies with court approval, and allows experts to use professional treatises.
162.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

163.title: Testimony to facts stated in document mentioned in section 162
163.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

164.title: Right of adverse party as to writing used to refresh memory
164.text: Requires documents used to refresh memory to be shown to the adverse party upon request, allowing cross-examination on their contents.
164.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

165.title: Production of documents
165.text: Mandates document production by summoned witnesses, with the court deciding objections, inspecting documents (except state matters), and ensuring confidentiality during translation, with protections for privileged communications.
165.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

166.title: Giving, as evidence, of document called for and produced on notice
166.text: Requires a party inspecting a document produced on notice to use it as evidence if demanded by the producing party, ensuring fairness in document use.

167.title: Using, as evidence, of document production of which was refused on notice
167.chapter: Chapter X: Of Examination of Witnesses (Sections 140-168)

168.title: Judge’s power to put questions or order production
168.text: Grants judges broad authority to question witnesses or order document production to uncover relevant facts, with limits on compelling protected answers or documents and ensuring judgments rely on duly proved facts.

169.title: No new trial for improper admission or rejection of evidence

170.title: Repeal and savings
170.text: Provides a standardized template for summoning a witness to appear in court to give evidence or produce documents, with a warning of legal consequences for non-compliance, as referenced in Sections 65, 69, and 165.
